To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the folding mechanism of a protein can be understood by the examination of the free energies of partially folded microstructures.

(1) the folding of proteins can be predicted from knowledge of the free energy of formation of partially folded intermediates and (2) the folding of a protein with two symmetrical hairpins can proceed through an asymmetrical transition state if one hairpin has a lower free energy of formation than the other.

the folding mechanisms of protein L and G are determined by the strength of the hairpin interactions, and that the strength of hairpin interactions are determined by the free energy of the partially folded microstates.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of sequence in protein folding.
understanding how the sequence of amino acids affects folding.
the role of sequence in determining protein folding pathways.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the folding mechanism of protein L involves the formation of the N‐terminal β‐hairpin followed by the formation of a compact intermediate.
the folding transition state is a consequence of the free energy landscape of the folding pathway.
sequence determines topology, which in turn determines folding mechanism.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
protein folding is driven by the formation of the most stable intermediate.
the free energy of partially folded states is an important determinant of folding pathways.
the folding transition state is not determined by the native state, but rather by a series of microstates that are partially folded.
The main takeaway from our work is that
protein folding can be understood as a series of steps that are driven by the relative stability of the partially folded microstates.
the folding mechanism of a protein is not determined solely by its topology.
the folding of protein L is driven by the strength of interactions in the N‐hairpin and the folding of protein G is driven by the entropy associated with the C‐terminal region.
